content: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of severe side effects when using the contraceptive patch containing norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol. These risks include heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. Women over the age of 35 and those who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day) are at an even higher risk. If you use this contraceptive patch, you should not smoke. The norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal system, commonly referred to as the contraceptive patch, is prescribed to prevent pregnancy. Norelgestromin is a progestin, and ethinyl estradiol is an estrogen. These are two female sex hormones. The patch works by preventing ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries) and altering the cervical mucus and uterine lining to make it more difficult for sperm to reach the egg or for a fertilized egg to implant. While the patch is highly effective in preventing pregnancy, it does not protect against the transmission of HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. The contraceptive patch is applied to the skin and is used in a 4-week cycle. A new patch is applied once a week for three consecutive weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which menstruation typically occurs. It is essential to follow the instructions provided by your doctor or pharmacist carefully. If you are starting the patch for the first time, you may apply it on the first day of your menstrual period or the first Sunday after your period begins. If you start the patch after the first day of your period, you must use an additional method of birth control (such as condoms or spermicide) for the first seven days of the first cycle. Always apply the patch on the same day of the week, referred to as your Patch Change Day. During the fourth week, remove the patch and do not apply a new one. Begin a new 4-week cycle by applying a new patch the day after the fourth week ends, even if your period has not started or has not ended. Do not go more than seven days without wearing a patch. Apply the patch to clean, dry, intact, and healthy skin on the buttock, abdomen, upper outer arm, or upper torso, avoiding areas that may be rubbed by tight clothing. Do not place the patch on the breasts or on skin that is red, irritated, or cut. Avoid applying makeup, creams, lotions, powders, or other topical products to the area where the patch is placed. Rotate the application site with each new patch to minimize skin irritation. Do not cut, decorate, or alter the patch in any way, and do not use extra tape, glue, or wraps to secure it. To apply the patch, follow these steps: 1. Open the foil pouch by tearing along the edge. 2. Peel apart the foil pouch and lay it flat. 3. Use your fingernail to lift one corner of the patch and peel it, along with its clear plastic liner, off the foil liner. Be careful not to remove the clear liner while doing this. 4. Peel away half of the plastic liner, avoiding contact with the sticky side of the patch. 5. Apply the sticky side of the patch to your skin and remove the remaining half of the plastic liner. Press down firmly on the patch with the palm of your hand for 10 seconds, ensuring the edges stick well. 6. After one week, remove the patch, fold it in half so it sticks to itself, and dispose of it in a trash can out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush the patch down the toilet. Check the patch daily to ensure it is securely attached. If the patch becomes partially or completely detached for less than one day, try to reapply it immediately in the same location. If it is no longer sticky, has stuck to itself or another surface, or has any material stuck to it, apply a new patch instead. If the patch has been detached for more than one day or if you are unsure how long it has been detached, you may not be protected from pregnancy. Start a new cycle immediately by applying a new patch, which will become your new Patch Change Day. Use a backup method of birth control for the first week of the new cycle. If the skin under the patch becomes irritated, you may remove the patch and apply a new one to a different area of skin. Leave the new patch in place until your regular Patch Change Day. Always remove the old patch before applying a new one, as you should never wear more than one patch at a time. This medication may be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using the contraceptive patch, inform your doctor if you are allergic to estrogens, progestins, or any other medications. Also, let your doctor know if you are using any other hormonal birth control methods, such as pills, rings, injections, or implants. Your doctor will advise you on how and when to transition to the patch. Do not use other hormonal birth control methods while using the patch. Provide your doctor and pharmacist with a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Certain medications, such as antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medications, and others, may interact with the patch, requiring dose adjustments or careful monitoring for side effects. Inform your doctor if you are taking herbal products, especially those containing St. John’s wort. Notify your doctor if you have recently had surgery, are on bed rest, or have a history of conditions such as heart attack, stroke, blood clots, certain cancers, liver disease, or other significant medical issues. Your doctor may advise against using the patch if you have these conditions. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have recently given birth, had a miscarriage, or weigh 198 pounds or more, as these factors may affect the patch's effectiveness. If you become pregnant while using the patch, contact your doctor immediately. If you miss two consecutive periods while using the patch correctly, or one period if used incorrectly, consult your doctor to rule out pregnancy. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are using the patch. Your doctor may recommend discontinuing the patch several weeks before surgery. If you wear contact lenses and experience vision changes, consult an eye doctor. Be aware that the average estrogen levels in your blood may be higher with the patch than with oral contraceptives, potentially increasing the risk of serious side effects such as blood clots. Discuss the risks and benefits of the patch with your doctor to determine the best birth control method for you. Continue your normal diet unless otherwise instructed by your doctor. If you forget to apply a patch at the start of a cycle (Week 1, Day 1), apply it as soon as you remember. This will establish a new Patch Change Day and Day 1. Use a backup birth control method for one week. If you forget to change the patch during Week 2 or Week 3 for one or two days, apply a new patch immediately and continue with your usual Patch Change Day. If you forget for more than two days, start a new cycle immediately with a new patch and use backup birth control for one week. Mild side effects of the patch may include skin irritation, breast tenderness, nausea, weight changes, acne, and menstrual irregularities. Severe side effects, such as sudden headaches, chest pain, or vision changes, require immediate medical attention. The patch may increase the risk of certain cancers, gallbladder disease, liver tumors, heart attack, stroke, and blood clots. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store the patch in its original container, tightly closed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unused patches properly, and keep them out of reach of children. In case of overdose, remove all patches and contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Keep all medical appointments and undergo regular physical exams, including blood pressure checks and breast and pelvic exams. Inform laboratory personnel that you are using the patch, as it may interfere with certain tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refills.
